## Section 1: Market Overview

*Basis: the synthesis and website documents only. No web access. The profile gives no product description or named competitors, so the offer comes from the website and the competitor set is inferred. Confirm both against real deals.*

### 1. Overview (The "Why Now?")

Small and mid-sized companies are being told to "do something with AI." The usual answers are a large consulting engagement, a generic chatbot, or nothing. Large firms deliver board-level strategy at a price and pace that do not fit a 3 to 200 person company. Chatbots forget the business every time the tab closes ("Every chat starts from zero"). Staff are already using AI without a policy, so client data leaks and leaders have no view of the risk. Acme Advisory replaces these slow, expensive or unmanaged routes with senior, hands-on help plus tools the client owns.

The mission is to help leaders act faster: a clear AI roadmap in a 2-day workshop, a working AI "chief of staff" in three sessions, and a one-page AI use policy from seven questions. It is built to be easy to run:
- **Owned by the client.** Company knowledge sits in plain files the client keeps. The AI model can be swapped without losing anything.
- **Private by design.** Open-weight models run inside the client's own office, so client information stays there.
- **Fast to start.** The 10x Employee setup is described as about one hour. A booking link leads to an intro call.
- **Integration and API access:** Not available. The documents do not describe either.

The edge is the person behind it: a founder with about 25 years in business software who has run the product function and says he still builds AI agents.

### 2. Trends & Shifts In The Market

The documents describe these shifts through the site's own claims. They contain no regulatory research or adoption data, so treat the descriptions as the founder's point of view, not verified market facts.

| Shift Category | Description of Change | The Window of Opportunity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Unmanaged AI use at work | The site states "Your team is already using AI" on two pages. Staff adopt tools faster than leaders write rules. | A one-page policy plus a rollout kit gives owners control in days. A free generator is a low-friction way in. |
| Privacy and client confidentiality | Regulated professional firms (law, accounting, mortgage) cannot send client data to public AI tools. Open-weight models can now run inside a firm's own firewall. | Private AI for firms of about 3 to 25 people. It is the most defined offer, with a named buyer, size band and disqualifiers. Large firms rarely serve this size. |
| Model churn and lock-in fear | AI models change often. Leaders worry that work built on one model is lost when it changes. | Model-agnostic "company Brain" in plain files. The site's promise: "Change models next year and you lose nothing." |
| Build in-house over buy | The founder's "build trap" view: more teams are building AI themselves, and many stall without product discipline. | Operator-led advisory on what to build, what to skip and how to ship. This is where product experience counts. |
| Crowded, generic AI advice | The synthesis says most providers use generic "AI strategy and transformation" language. Market size estimates run roughly $5B to $11B in 2025, with growth of about 17% to 26% a year. Definitions differ by source. | Growth draws more entrants, so a narrow, specific offer stands out. Acme Advisory's serviceable share: Not available. |

### 3. Landscape Map & Differentiation

**Category Context:** Acme Advisory sits in AI consulting and advisory, with adjacent AI governance. It also ships small software tools and workshops, which blurs the category. The site has no single category claim. The header splits into "Advisory", "Products" and "Workshops". Brand awareness is low and unmeasured. The category needs one clear name before buyers can find the company.

**Alternative Comparison Table:**

| Alternate Solution | Status Quo Limitation | Core Limitation / Why We Win |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Strategy houses | Board-level brand and scale. Priced and paced for large enterprises. | Acme Advisory offers senior attention at lower cost and faster pace, for buyers too small to matter to them. |
| Large audit firms and systems integrators | Strong on governance, controls and scale. Heavy, slow engagements. | Smaller, bounded, hands-on work. The founder does the work himself. |
| Boutique AI and engineering firms | Build and engineering depth. Light on product, positioning and adoption. | Acme Advisory starts from what to build and how teams will use it, then helps them adopt it. |
| Solo fractional AI executives | Named senior operators with published fees and strong search presence. The closest rival's fees run from USD 80,000 for consulting, or USD 30,000 a month with a six-month minimum. | Opening for buyers below that price floor, or those who want independent, time-bound work. Acme Advisory pricing is mostly unpublished, so this edge is unproven. |
| AI governance software | Produces policies and tracking. Does not teach the team to use AI well. | Policy plus workshops plus working tools. A free policy generator covers the entry need. |
| Internal teams | Cheap in cash, slow in practice. Few small firms have anyone who has run AI adoption. | Operator experience in a short engagement, with tools the team keeps. |
| General chatbots and free chief-of-staff tools | Low cost, but no memory of the business and no privacy control. | A company Brain in client-owned files, usable across models, with a private deployment option. |

**Positioning Summary (Sweet Spot):**
- **Ideal customer (working hypothesis):** owners and CEOs of small, regulated or fast-growing firms who hold budget and authority, and who need AI to work safely without hiring a big firm. The best-defined slice is regulated professional firms of about 3 to 25 people. The founder must confirm which offer actually drives revenue.
- **Core edge:** an operator who has run the function, delivering bounded, private, client-owned AI work at a price and speed larger providers do not match.
- **Gaps to close before this holds:**
  - Proof: no case studies, logos or measured outcomes. Sources disagree on whether named testimonials exist.
  - Offer sprawl: three advisory lines, five products and two workshops, all delivered by one person.
  - Audience drift: the homepage speaks to product and revenue leaders, while most product pages speak to CEOs, owners and regulated firms.
  - Pricing opacity and undated workshops.
  - Certification wording: advise on readiness for an AI management standard, never imply the company can certify.

## Section 2: Target Customers

*Basis: the website crawl and the market overview. There are no customer interviews, deal records or named competitors in the inputs. Everything below is a hypothesis to confirm against real deals. ### ICP Statement

**Our ideal customers are owners and managing partners at regulated professional firms of roughly 3 to 25 people who struggle with staff already using public AI tools on client work, and are trying to get the productivity of AI without client information leaving the office.**

### Ideal Customer Profile

| Attribute | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Company Size** | Primary: 3 to 25 people, stated on the Private AI page. Secondary: "growing companies" and "any company that hires faster than it can explain itself". No headcount band is given for these. |
| **Industry/Vertical** | Primary: regulated professional firms. The site names law firms, accounting firms and mortgage brokers. Secondary: SaaS startups, and small and medium businesses in general. |
| **Geography** | Not available. The founder is likely based in Greater Vancouver, Canada, but the site does not say so. Assumed starting market: Canada, until deal data says otherwise. |
| **Key Roles** | Owner, managing partner, founder or CEO. The site says buyers have "the authority, the budget and the desire to move AI forward". Secondary: product leaders and revenue leaders, the homepage audience. |

### Segment Priority

| Priority | Segment | Why | Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Regulated firms, 3 to 25 people | Named buyer, size band, clear risk (client data) and a defined offer | Hypothesis. Confirm with deals. |
| 2 | CEOs and founders of growing companies | Fits the AI operating system, the AI workshops and the free tools. The size band is vague. | Hypothesis |
| 3 | Product and revenue leaders at SaaS companies | Fits the homepage headline and the advisory menu. Most product pages do not speak to them. | Hypothesis. Decide whether to keep. |

**Gap:** the homepage speaks to segment 3, while most product pages speak to segments 1 and 2. Pick one primary buyer and make the homepage match.

### Customer Jobs to be Done (JTBD)
- "Use AI to get more done without client information leaving our office."
- "Put a clear AI policy in front of staff that they will actually read, so we stop guessing who is using what."

- "Move AI forward in the business without hiring a full-time AI executive or paying large-firm fees."

| No written AI rules, or rules nobody reads. | A one-page policy from seven questions, plus what you need to roll it out. Staff know what is allowed. |

| Large firms are too expensive and too slow for a small business. | Senior, hands-on advice from someone who has run the function, at a scale that fits a small firm. |

*Pains and gains come from the website's own claims. None are backed by customer research or measured results. Not available: customer quotes about the pain in their own words.*

### Buying Triggers
*Inferred from website messaging. Not confirmed by deals.*

- **Trigger 1: Staff are already using public AI tools on client work.** The site's opener is "Your team is already using AI." A regulated firm that finds this out has a risk to fix.
- **Trigger 2: A client, insurer or regulator asks how the firm uses AI.** The firm needs an answer and a written policy. Confirm whether this has happened in real deals.
- **Trigger 3: Hiring outpaces the firm's ability to explain itself.** The site says "any company that hires faster than it can explain itself". Onboarding becomes the bottleneck.
- **Trigger 4: A leader tries AI, hits the chatbot ceiling and wants more.** This feeds the fluency workshop and the AI chief of staff.
- **Trigger 5: Planning season.** The accelerator is a 2-day offsite to build a 2027 AI roadmap. Dates are still to be announced.

### Gaps and Next Steps
- **Confirm the primary ICP** against the last 3 to 5 deals or conversations. Not available: customer count, revenue by offer.
- **Add proof for the primary segment.** The site shows no case studies, logos or measured outcomes. Two testimonials exist, but the research disagrees on their presence. One CEO anecdote is anonymous.
- **Define disqualifiers for each segment.** Only Private AI has them.
- **Interview 3 to 5 buyers** on what triggered the purchase and what else they considered. This replaces the inferred triggers and alternatives above.
- **Avoid certification claims.** Preparing a client for a standard is not the same as certifying them.

### Step B: Expand Each Value Driver

---

#### Value Driver: Use AI on Client Work Without Client Information Leaving the Office

1. **Customer Challenge:** The owner knows AI would help the team do more. The owner also knows staff are already pasting client material into public AI tools. Banning AI makes the firm fall behind. Allowing it freely puts client confidentiality at risk. The owner cannot see which tools are used or what goes into them.

2. **Status Quo:** The old way is one of three things.
   - Staff use public chatbots on their own, with no visibility.
   - The owner sends a vague "be careful" email.
   - The owner bans AI, and staff use it anyway.
   
   In all three, the firm has no control over where client data goes.

3. **Cost of Inaction:** *Not available: measured figures. The logic is as follows.*
   - Client data may already be sitting with outside AI providers. The firm cannot say which data, or how much.
   - One confidentiality incident can cost a client relationship. In a 3 to 25 person firm, one lost client is a visible share of revenue.
   - Competitors that adopt AI safely will turn work faster. A firm that bans AI loses on speed. A firm that allows it freely carries the risk.
   - Rep tip: ask the buyer to put a number on the annual value of their top three clients. That is the exposure.

4. **Our Distinct Advantage:** Private AI runs the models inside the client's own office, so client information stays there. It is built for firms of about 3 to 25 people, with a defined timeline and disqualifiers. Large integrators build for big organizations. Public tools cannot keep data in the office. Fractional AI executives usually advise and do not deliver a working private setup at this size. *Not stated on the site: whether other small-firm providers offer the same. Confirm before claiming "the only".*

5. **Future State:** The firm uses AI every day on real client work. Client information never leaves the office. The owner can say so with confidence. Staff get the productivity benefit without a ban. The owner stops guessing who is using what.

6. **Proof Points:**
   - **Design logic:** when the model runs inside the firm's own firewall, client data does not go to an outside provider. This follows from how the system works.
   - **Defined scope:** the offer states a buyer, a 3 to 25 person size band, a timeline and disqualifiers. This signals that it is a real, bounded engagement.
   - **Operator credibility:** the founder has about 25 years in business software and says he still builds AI agents. This is self-reported. The market overview notes a self-reported $1B exit at a prior company.
   - **Not available:** customer case studies, named firms, measured results, security review or third-party validation. This is the largest gap. Close it before the homepage leans on this driver.

7. **Discovery Prompts:**
   - "If you asked every person on your team today which AI tools they used on client work this week, how confident are you the answer would match what you think?"
   - "Think of your three most important clients. What would it cost you if one found out their material had been pasted into a public AI tool?"
   - "You can ban AI or allow it. What does each choice cost you over the next two years, against firms that find a safe third path?"

---

#### Value Driver: Give a Clear, Defensible Answer When Someone Asks How Your Firm Uses AI

1. **Customer Challenge:** A client, insurer or regulator will ask how the firm uses AI. The owner needs a straight answer backed by something written. Most small firms have no written rules, or have rules nobody has read. Without them, the owner cannot answer, and staff do not know what is allowed.

2. **Status Quo:** The old way is to improvise.
   - The owner writes a rushed answer when the question arrives.
   - A template is copied from the internet and filed.
   - Governance software produces a document, but behavior does not change.
   
   The policy exists on paper. Staff do not follow it, so it would not hold up if tested.

3. **Cost of Inaction:** *Not available: measured figures. The logic is as follows.*
   - An unanswered question from a client or insurer can delay or lose an engagement or a renewal. The firm cannot control when the question arrives.
   - Leadership time goes into emergency answers instead of work.
   - A policy that staff ignore is worse than none, because it creates a false sense of cover.
   - Rep tip: ask whether any client or insurer questionnaire in the past year had an AI question the firm could not answer cleanly. Confirm that this really happens in deals.

4. **Our Distinct Advantage:** Acme Advisory pairs a free AI Use Policy Generator (a one-page policy from seven questions) with hands-on help to roll it out so staff follow it. Software gives a template. Acme Advisory changes how the team works, and pairs the policy with a private AI setup that makes the safe path the easy path. The free tool is also a low-risk way for a buyer to try the approach before paying. *Not stated on the site: the contrast with governance software. Confirm before use.*

5. **Future State:** The owner has a short written policy that staff have read and follow. When a client, insurer or regulator asks, the owner answers in minutes with a real document and a real system behind it. AI use becomes a strength in the conversation, not a worry.

6. **Proof Points:**
   - **Low-friction proof:** the policy tool is free, so the buyer can see the quality of the thinking before any commitment.
   - **Simple by design:** seven questions and one page. Short policies are more likely to be read than long ones. This is reasoning, not measured data.
   - **Honest scope:** Acme Advisory prepares a firm for a standard. It does not certify a firm. Keep this line in all copy. Overclaiming here would damage trust with the regulated buyers this offer targets.
   - **Not available:** evidence that clients, insurers or regulators accepted a policy built this way, and any adoption rates.

7. **Discovery Prompts:**
   - "If a client emailed you tomorrow asking for your firm's AI policy, what would you send, and would your team be able to explain it?"
   - "When was the last time your staff read your AI rules? What happens to a rule nobody can recall?"
   - "If an insurer or regulator asked you to show how AI is controlled, would you be showing a document or showing how your team works?"

---

#### Value Driver: Make Your Firm's Knowledge Work for Every Person and Every AI Tool, Not Just the Owner

1. **Customer Challenge:** How the firm works lives in the owner's head and in a few senior people. Every new hire has to learn it from scratch. Every AI chat also starts from zero, so people re-explain the business again and again. This caps how fast the firm can grow and how useful AI can be.

2. **Status Quo:** The old way is word of mouth and scattered files.
   - New hires shadow senior staff for months.
   - Knowledge is spread across inboxes, shared drives and memory.
   - People re-type context into AI chats and get generic output.
   - If a firm does build something with one AI vendor, it can be stuck when models change.

3. **Cost of Inaction:** *Not available: measured figures. The logic is as follows.*
   - Each new hire costs senior time to train, and that time is taken from billable or revenue work.
   - The firm cannot hire faster than it can explain itself, so growth stalls at the owner's capacity.
   - If a key person leaves, the knowledge leaves with them.
   - Staff waste time re-explaining context to AI and get poor output, so the firm pays for AI and gets little from it.
   - Rep tip: ask for the time a new hire takes to become productive and what a senior person's hour is worth. Multiply by hires per year.

4. **Our Distinct Advantage:** 10x Employee builds one company knowledge base in plain files the client owns. Any AI tool can read it. Three things follow:
   - The firm owns the knowledge, so it does not leave with a person or a vendor.
   - The firm can swap AI models later and lose nothing.
   - AI starts with the firm's context, not from zero.
   
   The design is model-agnostic and owned by the client. *Not available: whether competing offers use the same approach. Confirm before claiming "only".*

5. **Future State:** A new hire starts with context from day one. Staff and AI tools work from the same source of truth. The owner is no longer the bottleneck. When a better AI model arrives next year, the firm switches without rebuilding anything.

6. **Proof Points:**
   - **Design logic:** plain files are readable by people and by most AI tools, which supports both the ownership and the no-lock-in claims.
   - **Related capability:** the AI Chief of Staff tool and Executive AI Fluency workshops show the same approach in use. Use them as a demo path, not as outcome proof.
   - **Operator credibility:** the founder is a product executive who ran the function and says he builds AI agents himself. This is self-reported.
   - **Not available:** customer results such as time to productivity, hours saved or onboarding comparisons. One anonymous CEO anecdote exists on the site, and the research disagrees on whether named testimonials exist. Do not cite either as proof until confirmed.

7. **Discovery Prompts:**
   - "Think about your last hire. How many weeks until they worked without checking with you, and what did those weeks cost?"
   - "If your two most senior people left next quarter, what would the firm no longer know how to do?"
   - "When your team uses AI today, how much of each conversation goes into explaining your business before the useful part starts?"

### Gaps and Next Steps

- **Rank the drivers by deal evidence.** The order above follows the ICP hypothesis. Check it against the last 3 to 5 conversations.
- **Replace reasoned costs with real ones.** Interview 3 to 5 buyers. Ask what triggered the purchase and what it cost them to wait.
- **Build proof first for Driver 1.** One anonymized case study with a clear outcome would do more than any new copy.
- **Confirm Driver 2's trigger.** Check whether clients, insurers or regulators have actually asked small firms about AI use.
- **Keep certification language careful.** Preparing a client for a standard is not certifying them.
- **Match the homepage to these drivers.** It now speaks to product and revenue leaders, while these drivers speak to owners of regulated firms.

| 2 | **A knowledge base the client owns, in plain files, that works with any AI model** | Providers that earn from lock-in will not build it. It also reduces ongoing platform revenue for whoever sells it. | Medium to high. Technically simple. The barrier is business incentive, not skill. |

### Moat 1: Private AI Sized for Small Regulated Firms

#### 1. Description of the Advantage
- **What it is:** AI models run inside the client's own office and firewall. Client information never goes to an outside AI provider. The offer is built for firms of about 3 to 25 people, with a stated buyer, timeline and disqualifiers.
- **The "Unfair" Element:**
  - Public AI tools cannot offer this. Their model is built on data leaving the office.
  - Large integrators and strategy houses build for big organizations. A 5-person law firm is not a viable engagement for them.
  - Fractional AI executives usually advise. They do not deliver a working private setup at this size.
  - **Honest limit:** the technique is not secret. A well-funded boutique could copy it. The edge is the tight fit between buyer, size band and a bounded offer. *Not available: whether other small-firm providers offer the same. Confirm before claiming "the only".*

#### 2. Why Customers Care (The "So What?")
- **Value Translation:**
  - The owner stops choosing between banning AI and risking client confidentiality.
  - Staff get the speed benefit of AI on real client work.
  - The owner protects the firm's core asset: client trust. Losing one client is a visible share of revenue at this size.
- **Strategic Shift:**
  - **Lagging:** the owner finds out after the fact what staff pasted into public tools, if they find out at all.
  - **Leading:** the owner knows where client data goes before anyone asks, because it does not leave the office.

#### 3. Proof Points
- **Design logic:** a model running inside the firm's own firewall does not send data to an outside provider. This follows from how the system works.
- **Bounded scope:** the offer states a buyer, a 3 to 25 person size band, a timeline and disqualifiers. This shows a real engagement, not open-ended consulting.
- **Operator credibility (self-reported):** about 25 years in business software, and the founder says he still builds AI agents himself.
- **Not available:** customer case studies, named firms, measured results, a security review or third-party validation. This is the largest gap in the moat.

#### 4. Discovery Prompts
- "If you asked each person on your team which AI tools they used on client work this week, how closely would the answers match what you expect?"
- "Which of your top three clients would be most upset to learn their material went into a public AI tool, and what is that relationship worth each year?"
- "When you compare banning AI with allowing it freely, which cost do you expect to be larger in two years, and what would a third option need to prove to you?"

---

### Moat 2: A Knowledge Base the Client Owns, Readable by Any AI Model

#### 1. Description of the Advantage
- **What it is:** One company knowledge base in plain files the client owns. Any AI tool can read it. It is the core of the 10x Employee offer.
- **The "Unfair" Element:**
  - Providers that earn from lock-in have a reason not to build this. Making the client portable cuts their own recurring revenue.
  - Structure and ownership sit with the client. The client leaves with the knowledge if the engagement ends. A vendor built on retention finds that hard to offer.
  - **Honest limit:** plain files are easy to produce. The edge is the incentive and the willingness to give the asset away, plus the senior judgment on what to capture. *Not available: whether competing offers use the same approach. Confirm before claiming "the only".*

#### 2. Why Customers Care (The "So What?")
- **Value Translation:**
  - A new hire starts with context on day one. Less senior time goes to training, and that time returns to billable or revenue work.
  - Staff stop re-explaining the business in every AI chat and get useful output sooner.
  - Knowledge no longer leaves with a key person or a vendor.
  - When a better AI model arrives, the firm switches and rebuilds nothing.
- **Strategic Shift:**
  - **Lagging:** the firm learns what it lost only after a key person leaves or a vendor changes terms.
  - **Leading:** the firm's knowledge is captured and portable before either event.

#### 3. Proof Points
- **Design logic:** plain files can be read by people and by most AI tools. This supports both the ownership claim and the no-lock-in claim. A buyer can check this by opening the files.
- **Working demonstrations:** the free AI Chief of Staff tool and the Executive AI Fluency workshops use the same approach. Use them as a demo path, not as outcome proof.
- **Operator credibility (self-reported):** the founder ran the product function at software companies and builds AI agents himself.
- **Not available:** time to productivity, hours saved or onboarding comparisons from a real client. One anonymous CEO anecdote exists on the site. Do not cite it as proof until confirmed.

#### 4. Discovery Prompts
- "If your two most senior people left next quarter, which parts of how you work would nobody else be able to explain?"
- "If your current AI provider changed its pricing or terms next year, what would you lose, and what would it cost you to move?"
- "When someone new joins, where do they learn how you actually do things, and who owns that material today?"

---

### Moat 3: A Policy Staff Follow, Backed by a System That Makes It Easy

#### 1. Description of the Advantage
- **What it is:** Acme Advisory pairs the free AI Use Policy Generator (a one-page policy from seven questions) with hands-on rollout. It then ties the policy to a private AI setup. The safe path becomes the easy path.
- **The "Unfair" Element:**
  - Governance software produces a document. It does not change how a team works.
  - Build-focused firms deliver systems but often skip the written rules and the behavior change.
  - Acme Advisory owns both halves: the rule and the setup that makes the rule easy to follow. A competitor would need both skills in one delivery team.
  - **Honest limit:** the free tool is easy to imitate. The hands-on rollout depends on one person, which is both the quality and the scaling limit. *Not stated on the site: the contrast with governance software. Confirm before use.*

#### 2. Why Customers Care (The "So What?")
- **Value Translation:**
  - When a client, insurer or regulator asks about AI use, the owner answers in minutes with a real document and a real system.
  - Leadership time stops going into emergency answers.
  - A short policy that staff read removes the false cover of a policy nobody follows.
- **Strategic Shift:**
  - **Lagging:** the firm writes its answer after the question arrives, with a deadline running.
  - **Leading:** the firm has a working policy and system ready, so AI use becomes a point of strength in the conversation.

#### 3. Proof Points
- **Low-friction proof:** the policy tool is free. A buyer can judge the quality of the thinking before paying anything.
- **Simple by design:** seven questions, one page. Short policies are more likely to be read. This is reasoning, not measured data.
- **Honest scope:** Acme Advisory prepares a firm for a standard. It does not certify a firm. Keep this line in all copy.
- **Not available:** evidence that a client, insurer or regulator accepted a policy built this way, and adoption rates.

#### 4. Discovery Prompts
- "If a client emailed you tomorrow asking for your AI policy, what would you send, and could each person on your team explain it?"
- "Think of a rule your firm wrote in the past two years. How would you know whether people still follow it?"
- "If an insurer asked you to show how AI is controlled, would you be handing over a document or showing how your team works?"

---

### Moat Strength Check

| Test | Moat 1 | Moat 2 | Moat 3 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Backed by customer proof | No | No | No |
| Hard for large providers to copy | Yes. Size band is uneconomic for them. | Partly. Incentive blocks them. | Partly |
| Hard for small boutiques to copy | No. Fit and speed are the edge. | No. Incentive and judgment are the edge. | Partly. Needs governance and delivery together. |
| Depends on the founder | Yes | Yes | Yes |

**Read this honestly:** none of the three is a technical lock. The real moat is a combination: one senior operator, one defined buyer, and an offer that gives control to the client. That combination is hard to copy. It is also hard to scale, because every delivery depends on one person.

---

### Gaps and Next Steps

- **Lead with Moat 1.** It has the most defined buyer and the sharpest pain. Moats 2 and 3 support it.
- **Build one anonymized case study first.** Show a firm, a before state, an after state and one measurable outcome. This does more for all three moats than any new copy.
- **Get a security review or written technical description** of how Private AI keeps data in the office. Without it, Moat 1 is a claim, not proof.
- **Confirm uniqueness before using "only".** Check what other small-firm providers, governance tools and build-focused firms actually offer. Use "built for" or "designed for" until then.
- **Decide how the moat scales.** Founder dependency is the main risk. Document the method so delivery does not rest on one person's time.
- **Keep certification language careful.** Preparing a client for a standard is not certifying them.

### 4. How to Win (Battlecard Summary)

#### A. The Global Network
- **When we win:** The buyer is a small or mid-size leadership team that needs AI decisions in weeks, wants a named senior advisor, and cannot justify enterprise programs. We are also the obvious pick when independence matters or the buyer wants plain advice on AI use, not a controls framework.
- **When they win:** The buyer is a large enterprise, the audit committee or board wants a recognized name, or AI governance sits inside an existing audit relationship. Expect heavy resistance on brand safety. Do not compete on scale.

#### B. The Fractional Bench
- **When we win:** The buyer needs AI as a priority, not one more fractional seat. We win with a clear price range, a standards-based governance path and hands-on adoption with staff, none of which its CAIO page shows.
- **When they win:** The buyer wants several fractional roles at once (for example finance, technology and AI), or a private equity sponsor wants one provider across a portfolio. Be cautious when the buyer values a long track record over AI depth.

#### C. The Compliance Specialist
- **When we win:** The buyer has no certificate deadline and wants AI to create value: where to use it, who owns it, how teams adopt it, and how it affects sales. We also win as the independent advisor who prepares the buyer before any audit.
- **When they win:** A customer or contract demands an ISO 42001 or similar certificate, and the buyer wants audit, testing and tooling from one provider. Expect resistance when the question is "who can certify us fastest". Consider partnering with an accredited body instead of competing.

#### D. The Solo Fractional CAIO
- **When we win:** The buyer is under his USD 80,000 floor, wants a bounded engagement, needs hands-on adoption help, or wants advice from someone with no implementation stake. Confirm Acme Advisory's own price and terms before using this story.
- **When they win:** The buyer is a mid-market or enterprise CEO with budget, wants a standing executive seat, and values his stated record running AI in his own companies. Expect resistance if he is already on the shortlist. Do not claim "named senior advisor" as a unique edge, because he sells the same thing. Compete on fit, scope and independence, and do not attack his published fees, which are a real strength.

**Gaps to close**

**Questions to ask each client for a usable proof point**
